title: AI Literacy: The Immediate Need and What it Includes
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard argues that students and educators need AI literacy before the next school year, both to use tools properly and to live well in an AI world. He surveys the literature that defined the term and then lays out the literacies he thinks students need: basic understanding of what AI is and how language models work, practical use such as prompting and managing hallucinations, societal impacts like employment disruption, deepfakes, manipulation and cyberbullying, broader ethical issues, questions about what makes us human, the benefits, and human-AI collaboration. His school-specific claims are that bans widen inequity, that single-artifact assessments are being disrupted, and that students are being punished for misuse they were never taught to avoid. Note that he also advertises his own AI literacy course.
points: AI literacy covers basics, practical use, societal impacts, ethics, benefits and human-AI collaboration, not just tool operation.
Students are often left to learn AI tools with no guidance and sometimes punished for improper use they were never taught to avoid.
School bans on generative AI may widen the gap between students with private access and those without it.
Single-artifact assessments such as essays are becoming easier for AI to produce and harder for teachers to detect.
Without AI literacy, students risk treating chatbots as friends rather than as fallible tools.
quotes: While there is some argument over the details of where this technology will take us and how quickly we will get there, there is little doubt that this technology will have a dramatic impact on the world, and it already has.

While it is not important to know the technical details of how large language models work, it is useful to understand the basics of how they function so the strengths and weaknesses can be understood. They are useful for many things, but there is no way for them to reliably produce facts absent a significant change in their architecture.

Students need to understand that if they are going to learn foundational academic knowledge and skills they will need in life, they still need to do the work in a way that is consistent with the school and/or classroom policy. Currently, students are often struggling to learn how to use AI tools without any guidance, are often using them improperly, and are sometimes even punished for their use even though they have not been taught to properly use them.

Generative AI bans in schools are arguably widening the gap between private schools that are allowing access and public schools that are denying it. The reality is that only the least well-off students who cannot access ChatGPT on any other device or network are excluded from the AI world.

New AI tools have significant potential to disrupt education because students are currently assessed based on many single artifact assessments (research papers, essays) that can be written more and more by AI tools. The quality of the output produced by AIs will only increase over time and the ability of teachers to determine if it was written by AIs is rapidly declining, as AIs can be trained to write in the student’s own voice.

Perhaps we should think of AI as our children (Kellis) or our interns (given their current level of intelligence, Mollick), but they are not search engines. Students, at a minimum, are going to think of these bots as their tutors, and without AI literacy, we risk them thinking of them as their close friends.
